digests.narrative:
His core theme, and the week it stopped needing his advocacy. He reads a chain of independent confirmations as one story: AXT reporting the largest indium phosphide price hike on record — a fourth consecutive quarterly increase, with suppliers saying that even with money you may not get material — Elazr's GM telling an investor conference that the entire supply chain is out of stock and expecting the shortage to run for years across laser chip, PCB, carrier board and packaging, and AOI, Lumentum and MACOM all reporting the same imbalance from the earnings side.

His framing device is Nvidia as leading indicator. He argues Jensen telegraphs each theme roughly a year early and the market dismisses it every time: Nvidia bought EML and laser capacity in 2025 and the response was that photonics was a bubble; Nvidia is now locking CW and EML capacity with long-term agreements, pushing 800V, and being explicit about the CPO shift, and the response is that CW players are meme stocks. He expects the same resolution.

Within that he is hunting for who is left. Once Nvidia secures CW capacity he counts AOI, MACOM, Broadcom, Sivers and Semtech as the remaining Western CW players, and calls Sivers the highest-beta exposure and his personal long. On AOI specifically he is at maximum conviction after the Rosenblatt summit — US-production premiums on 800G and 1.6T, several LTAs declined so capacity is not blocked, sold out through at least H2 next year, and 40%+ margins once CPO arrives — while saying he wants a materially lower price before adding more.
keyPoints: InP substrate prices up a fourth consecutive quarter, the largest hike on record; epi wafer prices heading for a third increase
Elazr GM: the entire optical supply chain is out of stock and the shortage should last years
Nvidia telegraphs each theme a year early — CW capacity, 800V and CPO are the 2026 version of the 2025 EML trade
Sivers is his named highest-beta CW long; AOI his highest-conviction fundamental call, but he wants a much lower entry
AOI claims premiums for US 800G/1.6T production, sold out beyond next year, and 40%+ margins once CPO lands
He suspects photonics may echo the memory supercycle now that demand visibility runs multi-year

digests.narrative:
He is firmly against the view that the memory cycle is over, and this week he argued it from the NAND side rather than DRAM. Phison's CEO expects 2027 capacity constraints more severe than 2026, on the reasoning that upstream suppliers need up to four years from plant construction and equipment investment to actual production, so with demand growing explosively and supply expansion limited the shortage should last years.

SanDisk is his cleanest expression of it. He reads the investor day as removing the cyclicality argument outright: roughly 80% adjusted gross margins projected through 2030, around 75% operating margins and about 50% adjusted free cash flow margins, with long-term agreements already covering two thirds of 2028 output. He cites minimum contracted revenue reaching $93B against a market capitalisation near $239B and asks how a company with revenue targets running four years out can be called cyclical. He notes CXMT signing multi-year DRAM agreements as evidence the whole industry is converging on the same LTA playbook, and that conventional DRAM gross margins at Micron are estimated to reach an unprecedented level by 2027, surpassing HBM margins.

He is also extending the pattern outward. Watching AI-server MLCC lead times stretch — Samsung near 40 weeks, Murata moving 24 to 30 to 36 weeks, with new capacity postponed from Q4 2026 into 2027 — he expects the same crowding-out squeeze to hit consumer and general-purpose grades in late H2 or early 2027, explicitly comparing it to what happened to legacy DRAM.
keyPoints: Phison's CEO: 2027 NAND constraints more severe than 2026, with a multi-year shortage ahead
SanDisk investor day: ~80% adjusted gross margins through 2030, LTAs covering two thirds of 2028 output
He argues contracted revenue running to 2030 disqualifies the cyclical label
CXMT's multi-year DRAM agreements show the LTA playbook spreading across the industry
MLCC lead times stretching toward 40 weeks; he expects a legacy-DRAM-style crowding-out into 2027
He explicitly disagrees with the it's-all-over-for-memory crowd

digests.narrative:
TSMC sits at the centre of his map — he describes it plainly as the centre of the AI buildout — and he uses it more as a source than as a trade, quoting it on memory and ABF substrate tightness over the coming years and naming it as the capacity provider behind the rest of the chain.

GlobalFoundries is the one he argues actively. He points to the US government taking a material stake and expects co-packaged optics to re-accelerate revenue, and earlier expressed surprise the stock stayed down given a direct government stake intended to advance CPO — reading it as good news that went unrewarded. It also appears in his Sivers case as the photonic foundry partner spanning NPO, pluggable and CPO architectures.

Samsung Foundry raising prices roughly 10-15% is noted as part of the same tightening, and he tracks Chinese capacity separately: YMTC pursuing an IPO next quarter after CXMT's successful listing, with the Chinese IPO market running hot from Unitree through to memory makers.
keyPoints: He calls TSMC the centre of the AI buildout and cites it on memory and ABF substrate tightness
GlobalFoundries: a material US government stake plus CPO should re-accelerate revenue
GF also appears as the photonic foundry partner in his Sivers thesis across NPO, pluggable and CPO
Samsung Foundry price hikes of roughly 10-15% read as further tightening
YMTC pursuing an IPO next quarter following CXMT, with the Chinese listing market running hot

digests.narrative:
His neocloud argument this week is a rebuttal rather than a promotion. CoreWeave signing contracts for six-year-old Nvidia A100 GPUs running through 2029 is, on his read, a direct counterargument to the GPU depreciation short thesis — if hardware that old still clears multi-year contracts, the aggressive depreciation schedules the bears model are wrong, and that reads positive for Nebius and IREN as much as for CoreWeave.

Beyond that he groups the neoclouds with the other names where demand visibility now runs years rather than quarters, mentioning Nebius in the same breath as AOI in lasers and SanDisk in memory as businesses where the order book extends far enough to change how they should be valued.
keyPoints: CoreWeave contracting six-year-old A100s through 2029 rebuts the GPU depreciation short thesis
He reads that as positive for Nebius and IREN, not just CoreWeave
Neoclouds grouped with lasers and memory as multi-year demand-visibility stories
The depreciation debate, not demand, is the argument he thinks the bears are getting wrong

digests.narrative:
Substrates are where he thinks the shortage is most visible and least priced. He posted the indium phosphide story as the clearest evidence yet: prices began rising in Q4 last year and the latest increase is the fourth consecutive one, expected to exceed 10%, while epitaxial wafer prices made from those substrates have already risen twice and are heading for a third increase. His favourite detail is a supplier saying that even if you have the money, you still may not be able to get the material.

He claims the call — he predicted the squeeze last year — and holds both AXT and IQE, saying his February IQE thesis was validated alongside AXT and that he remains long both. He notes the reporting is Taiwan-centric and names VPEC, Landmark and IET as beneficiaries, and treats MACOM's long-term epiwafer agreements and equity stake in IQE as a soft backstop that reads positive for IQE specifically.

On packaging he holds Amkor as a duration bet rather than a momentum one — bought on post-earnings weakness he found surprising given the Nvidia deal and a ten-year TSMC agreement, and explicitly described as more of a 2028 name with a separate 2027 ramp. Applied Materials raising advanced packaging growth guidance and extending customer discussions to 2030 supports the direction.
keyPoints: InP substrate prices up for a fourth consecutive quarter, the latest hike expected above 10%
Epitaxial wafer prices already raised twice, moving toward a third increase
Suppliers reportedly telling customers that money alone will not secure material
He is long both AXT and IQE and says he called the squeeze a year early
The cited reporting credits Taiwanese players VPEC, Landmark and IET as beneficiaries
Amkor held as a 2028 duration bet backstopped by Nvidia and a ten-year TSMC agreement

digests.narrative:
Marvell is the name that moved his view this week. Google taking a warrant over $12.2B of Marvell stock as part of a custom-silicon agreement covering TPU-adjacent processors, storage controllers, network interface controllers and memory interfaces is read as potentially translating into around $120B of revenue through 2033. Combined with Amazon's separate warrants following the Celestial acquisition, he concludes Marvell has been quietly networking its way into every hyperscaler, and revisits Jensen's comment that Marvell would be the next trillion-dollar company as evidence Nvidia saw it first. He also expects Marvell to benefit most from the Maia 300 ramp.

On Semtech he is deliberately non-committal, which is worth recording because it is rare. He says he has no strong directional opinion and has not modelled it recently, but argues the architecture debate matters less there than elsewhere: whatever wins between LPO, LRO, NPO and CPO, all of them require TIAs and drivers, and AOI has said TIAs and DSPs were bottlenecked enough to limit its own transceiver output. With CPO, Semtech gets TIAs and drivers plus its HiFo CW opportunity, though he has not seen much on how those CW lasers are progressing.
keyPoints: Google's Marvell warrant spans TPU compute, storage, networking and memory interfaces
He sizes the implied opportunity near $120B of revenue through 2033
Amazon holds separate Marvell warrants post-Celestial, so multiple hyperscalers are contracted in
Marvell should benefit most from the Maia 300 ramp
On Semtech he explicitly declines a directional view — TIAs and drivers are needed across every architecture

digests.narrative:
This card changes shape this week: LPKF moves into the glass layer from materials, so the theme finally contains the name through which glass-substrate progress actually reaches the book. It is still only two tickers.

The news is a delay, and it is the analyst reporting a setback in his own theme, which is the kind of disclosure worth weighting heavily. Samsung Electro-Mechanics has delayed its semiconductor glass substrate investment on a bottleneck in customer reliability evaluations of prototypes, revising the start of operations to 2028, with SKC also pushing back. For an equipment supplier this is worse than it is for a substrate maker: the tool order lands before the line runs, so a customer moving its start date right moves LPKF's revenue with it, and there is no partial credit. The share price is down about 12% on the month, which is the market reading the same thing.

Corning remains the other half of the card and has not moved: its glass-bridge case rests on 2028 fibre array unit TAM rather than anything shipping, and co-packaged optics delay reports weigh on that and the FAU case together. Conviction stays low. Glass is a 2028-2029 layer on current evidence, and the datapoint that would change this card is a disclosed tool order from a named substrate customer with a delivery year attached — not another timeline article.
keyPoints: LPK.DE re-categorised into glass from materials — the layer now holds the equipment exposure directly
Samsung Electro-Mechanics delays glass substrate start of operations to 2028; SKC also pushes back
Equipment leads the line, so a customer's slip moves LPKF's revenue event with it
LPK.DE is down about 12% on the month against a flat tape
GLW's glass-bridge case still rests on 2028 FAU TAM rather than current shipments
What would change the card: a disclosed LIDE order from a named customer with a delivery year

digests.narrative:
The Unitree listing is the event he has been waiting for. Unitree went public and closed far above its IPO valuation, and he reads that as a major public benchmark proving demand for pure-play humanoid exposure is much larger than public markets expected. He has been tracking the oversubscription and the derivatives-implied opening for days beforehand, and frames China as currently leading the hardware race — citing Unitree claims that their humanoids now run faster than Usain Bolt and jump higher than any human.

Agility is his US expression, held through the Churchill vehicle. He bought between 0.25% and 0.75% of the float around announcement and expects the Unitree listing and other Chinese IPOs to lift it, since Agility has lagged its expected opening valuation. His operating argument is that Agility targets commercialisation first — Digit inside Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouses — and that delivery and packaging robots do not need to do backflips, making Boston Dynamics the closer peer for capability and Agility the closer peer for revenue. He explicitly excludes Tesla as the pure-play: Optimus sits inside a company worth over a trillion dollars, and he does not think Tesla can pull off general-purpose robotics yet.

On components he is more cautious than the theme suggests. Harmonic, LeaderDrive and Schaeffler appear almost everywhere — Schaeffler claims work with around 45 humanoid players — and smaller suppliers are niche possibilities, but he expects Chinese suppliers into Agibot and Unitree to book revenue first.
keyPoints: Unitree's listing gives humanoids their first major public benchmark, far above its IPO valuation
He holds Agility via the Churchill vehicle, bought at 0.25-0.75% of float, expecting a read-across
Agility targets commercial logistics in Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouses, not general-purpose capability
He rules Tesla out as the pure-play: Optimus is wrapped inside a company far too large
Component exposure is thin and Chinese suppliers to Agibot and Unitree likely book revenue first
China currently leads the humanoid hardware race on his read

digests.narrative:
Nvidia is less an investment case for him than an information source. His argument is that AI investing is simpler than people expect because Nvidia and Jensen tell everyone what is coming, and markets dismiss it almost every time until it happens. He tracks the forward commitments closely: SB Energy talks, a compute financing push above $500B, Feynman on A16 with custom HBM and co-packaged optics, and an 800VDC MGX rack.

On AMD he is constructive for structural reasons rather than valuation ones — Helios plus the CPU line should bring another inflection point, and he notes approvingly that AMD is copying Nvidia's neocloud flywheel by helping fund raises that turn into AMD GPU purchases. He frames it as a second rack-scale accelerator family existing at all, which changes the supplier arithmetic beneath it.

What he does not do is argue accelerators on price. The layer functions in his framework as the demand hub whose forward statements validate positions further down the chain.
keyPoints: His core method: treat Nvidia's forward statements as a leading indicator the market discounts
Feynman on A16 with custom HBM and CPO, plus the 800VDC MGX rack, are the next telegraphed themes
AMD's Helios and CPU line should drive another inflection point
AMD copying the neocloud fundraise-into-GPU flywheel is read as a structural positive
He rarely argues this layer on valuation — it is the demand signal for the layers beneath

digests.narrative:
He treats the hyperscalers primarily as demand signals rather than positions, and this week almost every mention pointed at a supplier instead. Amazon's ASIC programme is ramping and he says the Trainium ramp is arriving right about now — but the position he names is Alchip, not Amazon. Microsoft's Maia 300 capacity is being discussed with an unveil expected soon, and the bullish read he draws goes to Marvell rather than Microsoft.

The exception is the custom-silicon warrant structure, which he finds genuinely revealing. Google taking options over $12.2B of Marvell across TPU compute, storage controllers, network and memory interfaces — potentially translating into roughly $120B of revenue through 2033 — plus Amazon's separate Marvell warrants after the Celestial acquisition, is read as confirmation that the hyperscalers are contracting their way into their silicon suppliers. He connects it back to Jensen's remark that Marvell would be the next trillion-dollar company, arguing Nvidia saw Marvell networking its way into all of them.

The practical conclusion he keeps returning to is that hyperscaler capex is best owned through the bottleneck, not through the buyer.
keyPoints: He reads hyperscaler capex as a demand signal and consistently names the supplier as the position
Google's $12.2B Marvell warrant spans TPU compute, storage, networking and memory interfaces
Amazon holds separate Marvell warrants following the Celestial acquisition
Trainium ramping now, with Alchip named as the expression rather than Amazon
Maia 300 capacity discussed at Microsoft, with the bullish read going to Marvell

digests.narrative:
This layer exists because the desk built it, not because the feed produced it. Every thesis that touches power reaches it through a list rather than an argument. Bloom Energy is the only sustained name: it appears in a late-July recap for 166% year-on-year revenue growth with expanding margins and raised 2026 guidance, and again in the note that grid power bottlenecks triggered a five-fold increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for its fuel cells. That financing line is the clearest power-constraint datapoint anywhere in the feed.

The second thread is a components one and sits mostly outside the US listed set: a shortage of high-power cylindrical cells for battery backup units, with Samsung SDI supplying Simplo, which assembles for Meta and Amazon, and both Panasonic and Samsung reported short. Vertiv, Eaton, EnerSys and BorgWarner are named only as adjacent read-throughs, and the analyst says plainly it is outside his domain.

GE Vernova and Constellation carry no analyst mentions at all, which is exactly the tiering caveat this layer was built to expose: grid interconnection, transformers and on-site generation are load-bearing for every gigawatt in the neocloud and hyperscaler digests, and the feed prices none of it. Conviction is low because the evidence is thin, not because the constraint is.
keyPoints: Desk-built layer: no thesis in the feed argues power directly, only in passing
BE is the only sustained name — 166% YoY revenue growth, raised 2026 guidance
Grid power bottlenecks drove a 5x increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for BE fuel cells
A BBU cylindrical-cell shortage runs through Samsung SDI, Panasonic and Murata, with no direct US listing
VRT, ETN and ENS appear only as adjacent read-throughs, explicitly outside the analyst's domain
GEV and CEG carry zero analyst mentions, so they cannot rise above radar however load-bearing they are
